post.description:
Create an account and return a token for it.

Returns the token, so registering logs you in -- there is no useful state
in which an account exists and its owner is not signed in to it.

Exchange an address and password for a token.

One message for both "no such account" and "wrong password", and the
password is verified even when the account does not exist, so the two
cannot be told apart by what comes back or by how long it took. Otherwise
this endpoint is a way to find out who has an account here.

get.description: Who the caller is. The client's way to check a stored token still works.

post.description:
Change your own password, proving you know the current one.

Requiring the current password is not ceremony: without it, a token left
behind on a shared machine is enough to lock its owner out of their own
account permanently.

get.description: What the sign-in page can offer. Open: it is read before anyone signs in.

post.description:
Email a one-hour reset link to the address, if it has an account.

The same answer whether or not it does, for the reason login gives one
message for both: otherwise this is a way to find out who has an account.

Set a new password with a reset link's token, and sign in.

Signing in is what the person was trying to do when they found they could
not, so the response is the same as login's.

get.description: Your personal access tokens, newest first.

post.description:
Make a personal access token. The secret is in this response and nowhere
else: it is not stored, so it cannot be shown again.

delete.description: Revoke a token. It stops working at once; the row goes with it.

get.description:
Every curve available for calibration, in the order they should be
offered. This is the list the frontend's curve pickers are built from,
which is why archived curves are left out by default: they still resolve,
so old analyses rerun, but they are not offered for new work.

post.description:
Store a previewed curve.

Takes the file again rather than the rows the preview returned. Sending
the parsed numbers back would make the client a second, unvalidated route
by which curve data could reach the database -- the arrangement
api/imports.py's docstring argues against at length. Re-parsing costs
milliseconds and cannot disagree with the preview.

`async def` for the upload read only; the parse and the insert are
handed to the threadpool, for the reason preview_curve above gives.

get.description:
Two curves on one grid, with their difference.

The difference is the point. Drawn over each other, two calibration curves
look alike at any zoom that fits a millennium on screen; the hemispheric
offset between IntCal20 and SHCal20 is a few decades against an axis
spanning thousands of years. As A - B it reads immediately.

Declared before /curves/{curve_id} on purpose: routes match in declaration
order, and "compare" is a perfectly good curve id as far as the path
pattern is concerned, so the other way round this endpoint is a 404 for a
curve that does not exist.
One curve's full description, including its measured metadata.

patch.description:
Correct a stored curve's description, citation or aliases.

Its numbers are not editable here and never will be: an analysis already
run against this curve has to keep meaning what it said. Importing a
corrected file creates a new curve.

delete.description:
Remove a stored curve, or archive it.

A curve something has been calibrated against is refused, and the refusal
names what is using it: deleting it would leave saved results that can be
displayed but never reproduced. Archiving is the way out -- the curve
leaves every picker but still resolves, so those analyses still rerun.

get.description:
Curves of one display type ('terrestrial', 'marine',
'southern_hemisphere'). An unknown type is an empty list, not a 404: it
is a filter that matched nothing, not a missing resource.

A drawable slice of a curve: [cal BP, 14C age, 1-sigma, slope] rows.

Windowed and decimated server-side, because the browser asks for this again
on every zoom and a 9,501-point payload per zoom step would be wasteful --
and because the decimation has to be min/max per bucket (see
services/curve_view) rather than every Nth point, which is a decision that
belongs with the curve rather than with whichever client is drawing it.

post.description:
What a date from a given calendar year would look like.

The curve's own radiocarbon age at that year, calibrated back through the
curve with the stated laboratory error -- OxCal's C_Simulate, without its
random scatter. Deliberately without: a drawn measurement answers "what
might one particular sample give", which is a different question every
time it is asked, where this answers "how well does this year date", which
is the question a curve browser is for. It is also the single-date
counterpart of the aggregate the resolution panel reports.

get.description:
The visible window as CSV, so a stretch of curve can leave this app as
data rather than only as a picture.

How tightly a date from each calendar age could be known, before anyone
measures anything -- Svetlik et al. (2019); see services/resolution.py.

Each point is [cal BP, mean resolution, 5th percentile, 95th percentile,
laboratory sigma assumed], all in years. The percentiles are the spread
over what a single date might return: how lucky or unlucky one measurement
of a sample from that year can be.

parameters.name: u0

schema.description: Laboratory 1-sigma at 0 BP, scaled with age from there
schema.title: U0

parameters.description: Laboratory 1-sigma at 0 BP, scaled with age from there

get.description:
The whole curve's resolution profile as a CSV, in the column order res14c
publishes so the two can be compared directly.

post.description:
Read an uploaded curve file and report what it holds, storing nothing.

An unreadable file still answers 200: the request succeeded, and its
answer is the list of what is wrong. `data.ok` carries the verdict, and
`data.preview` a downsampled series so the dialog can draw the curve
before it is accepted.

One of the three handlers that must stay `async def`, since reading an
upload is genuinely awaitable. Everything after that read is parsing --
a whole .14c file's worth -- so it goes to the threadpool rather than
running on the event loop. See _preview_curve.

Define a curve as a proportional mixture of two others, for samples whose
carbon came from more than one reservoir -- most often a human or animal
with a partly marine diet, whose bone is neither terrestrial nor marine
carbon and is wrong by centuries against either curve alone.

Stored as the recipe, not as the resulting numbers: it stays honest about
its parents, and they count as in use for as long as it exists.

get.description:
What is already calibrated against this curve. Empty for a curve
nothing uses, which is the only kind that can be deleted outright.

`in_use` counts EVERY user's work, because that is what decides whether the
curve may be deleted. The id lists hold only this user's own analyses and
projects; everyone else's are reduced to `others_count`, so the answer is
complete without handing one user a list of another's row ids. See
curve_registry.usage.

post.description: Bring an archived curve back into the pickers.

get.description:
The curve as a .14c file.

An imported curve comes back byte-for-byte as it was uploaded -- that is
what storing the source text rather than a parsed array buys, and it means
a curve can leave this app in exactly the state it arrived. Anything else
(a builtin, later a mixed curve) is rendered from its points into the same
format.

post.description:
Calibrate a single radiocarbon measurement. The body is validated by
CalibrateRequest (schemas/sample.py).

Beyond the measurement it accepts project_id, which files the saved
analysis under a project (omitting it leaves the analysis unassigned but
still listed), and save, which when False writes nothing to the database
for a quick test run and returns a null "id".

Calibrate several measurements independently -- each exactly as
/analysis/calibrate would alone -- and save them as one analysis so they
share the Results page's plot and table in chronological order.

Where a Bayesian analysis asks what the dates imply together given their
stratigraphy, this lays independent dates out on one timeline with no
relationship asserted. Always saved: a set of dates worth calibrating
together is normally worth keeping.

Whether these measurements could all date one event (Ward and Wilson
1978; services/statistics.same_event), with the pooled age calibrated
where they pass. Nothing is saved: the model editor asks it of a Phase's
dates, before the run, to decide whether they are separate events or one
event to pool first.

Perform Bayesian chronological analysis.

The inputs are validated and persisted in THIS request -- so a malformed
model still answers 422 immediately, as it always did -- and the solve is
then queued, answering 202 with a job_id to poll at
GET /api/jobs/{job_id}. See docs/ASYNC_JOBS_PLAN.md.

Two cases stay synchronous. `wait=true` asks for it (see
rerun_analysis), and `save=false` has no choice: nothing is persisted, so
there is no analysis for a later poll to fetch results from and no row to
hang a job on. A quick test run is answered in full, as before.

The request body is validated by BayesianRequest (schemas/sample.py).

Accepts the same project_id / save options as /analysis/calibrate. With
save=False the run still happens in full -- there is no way to preview a
Bayesian result without running it -- and only the database writes are
skipped.

get.description: Retrieve analysis results

delete.description:
Permanently delete an analysis and everything tied to it. Unlike project
deletion there is no "unassign and keep": a result has no meaning outside
its analysis.

SampleGroup, StratigraphicRelationship and ModelElement have no cascade at
either the ORM or the DB level, so everything is deleted explicitly in
dependency order: results and relationships, then samples, then groups,
then the analysis.

patch.description:
Update an analysis's project assignment and/or name. Pass
project_id: null to unassign it.

get.description:
List analyses, most recent first, across all projects by default. Pass
project_id to scope to one, or unassigned=true for those filed under none.

delete.description:
Permanently delete several analyses at once -- the project page's
"delete selected".

All-or-nothing on the ids, as for the collection's bulk delete: an id that
is not one of the caller's analyses fails the whole request, so a caller
never has to work out which of its ids went. Someone else's analysis
answers the same 404 as one that does not exist (auth.owned_or_404).

The ids travel in the body, not the query string, for the same length
reason as DELETE /projects/{id}/samples.

post.description:
Recompute a saved analysis's results in place from its own persisted
inputs -- same id and URL, old results replaced.

Queued rather than run here, since a Bayesian model takes tens of seconds
and can take minutes (docs/ASYNC_JOBS_PLAN.md): answers 202 with a job_id
to poll at GET /api/jobs/{job_id}.

`wait=true` runs it in the request and answers 200 when finished. Kept
permanently, because this app has no client library and anything
scripting it from outside a browser has no event loop to poll from.

put.description:
Replace an analysis's model structure (services/model_tree.py).

Body: {"model_tree": {...}, "sample_elements": {sample_id: element_id}}.
`sample_elements` reassigns which phase each date belongs to; dates left
out keep their current assignment.

Validated by model_tree.validate_tree before anything is written, so a
structurally impossible model is rejected with a 422 rather than
surfacing later as a confusing MCMC failure. Existing results are cleared
and status returns to 'pending', since they were computed under the
previous structure.

post.description:
Deep-copy an analysis's INPUTS into a new analysis, so a variant can be
built from an existing one -- "the same dates, but grouped differently".

`new_seed` gives the copy a fresh random seed (bayesian_config.seed) and
says so in its name: an independent replicate of a sampled run, to set
beside the original in Compare Results and see how far Monte Carlo error
moves its figures. Only for a Bayesian analysis, the only kind that
samples.

`apply_inbuilt` sets the copy's "Apply inbuilt-age allowances" switch
(bayesian_config.apply_inbuilt) and says so in its name: the same model
with and without the dates' allowances, to compare side by side.

Copies the samples, contexts and stratigraphic relationships, remapping
ids to the new rows'. Results are NOT copied and status is 'pending', so
the copy can be edited (PUT /analysis/{id}/inputs) and then run
(POST /analysis/{id}/rerun).

put.description:
Replace a saved analysis's inputs -- measurements, contexts,
relationships, config -- wholesale: the "modify" half of
duplicate-and-modify.

Reuses BayesianRequest for validation, so an edit gets the same checks a
fresh analysis does: cycle detection, dangling references and TPQ/TAQ
contradictions are rejected with a 422 before anything is written.

Existing results are DELETED and each context's modelled start/end
cleared, since they came from the old inputs; status returns to 'pending'
until the analysis is re-run.

`analysis_type` in the body CONVERTS this analysis rather than creating a
second one. Omitting it leaves the type alone, which is what an ordinary
same-type edit means.

get.description:
Export results as a CSV table. Same content as /export/csv, kept as a
separate route for backwards compatibility.

Export an analysis's results as CSV, in the model's own reading order.

`date_format` (calBP / bcad / bce_ce) is the reporting format the results
page is showing; when it is not cal BP each calendar-age column gains a
formatted counterpart. An unrecognised value falls back to cal BP rather
than failing the download.

`p_before_bp` adds the results page's "P before" column, at that
threshold in cal BP, when the page is showing it.

Export an analysis's results as JSON, with sample details merged into
each result row.

Two views of the same data: `results` is the flat per-date list, and
`structure` is the same run in the model's own order, so a consumer can
reproduce the model rather than only the dates. Both come from one
assembly, so they cannot disagree; `structure` is empty for an analysis
with no stored structure.

The nested tree is not repeated here -- GET /api/analysis/{id} already
returns model_tree.

The probability each date and modelled parameter puts before `cal_bp`
(services/statistics.p_before), for the results page's "P before"
column. Read from the stored posteriors, so it answers for any analysis
without a re-run.

The analysis as an OxCal model file (services/oxcal_export.py): its
dates, curves, reservoir offsets, outlier settings and structure, for a
reader who runs OxCal. What OxCal's language there cannot carry is listed
in the file's header, and counted in the X-RadiCal-Not-Written header so
the page can say so.

Inputs only, so it is the same file before and after a run. An analysis
stored before model trees is written from the structure reading it would
build, without storing that.

Export an analysis as a printable PDF report: metadata, the curves and
solver that produced it, the results table in reading order, each
context's modelled span, and a posterior plot per modelled parameter.

Built from the same assembly the CSV and JSON exports use, so the three
downloads cannot report different numbers. `date_format` is carried the
same way the CSV carries it, falling back to cal BP if unrecognised.

Rendering is synchronous and costs a matplotlib figure per modelled
parameter, so a large model takes a few seconds -- the thing to revisit
if models grow.

post.description: Export results in the specified format: 'csv', 'json' or 'pdf'.

get.description:
List all projects with the numbers the project grid ranks, sorts and draws
with, plus an 'Unassigned' count so the frontend can offer that bucket
alongside real projects.

Every number here comes from a grouped query over the whole table rather
than a query per project, so the page costs the same at four projects and
at four hundred.

post.description: Create a new project to group analyses under.

get.description: Retrieve a project and the analyses filed under it.

patch.description:
Rename a project, edit its description, or change one of its two
coordinate settings.

The settings are not metadata. `coordinate_precision` decides how
precisely this project's positions may leave the app in an export or a
figure, and `map_tiles_enabled` whether the map may ask a third-party tile
server for imagery of them. The schema's Literal is what keeps the first
to the four values the exporter can actually apply.

delete.description:
Delete a project. Its analyses are NOT deleted, only unassigned, so
results are never lost to a project being cleaned up.

The project's date COLLECTION is deleted with it via the cascade on
Project.samples: a collected date has no meaning outside its project, and
any analysis deployed from it holds its own copy of the values.

post.description:
Recompute every analysis in this project in place from its own persisted
inputs (analysis._rerun_analysis). One failure does not abort the rest;
failures are collected and reported back.

Queued rather than run here: a Bayesian run per analysis back to back
takes minutes, well past what a reverse proxy or browser will hold.
Answers 202 with a job_id whose detail carries {completed, total, failed}.
`wait=true` runs it in the request -- see analysis.rerun_analysis.

get.description:
The project as one zip (api/project_export.build_zip): every analysis's
Export JSON, what each was run from, the run its results came from, the
curves they need, the date collection and a summary table across them.
`date_format` and `p_before_bp` read as they do on a single analysis's
exports.

`analysis` (repeatable) narrows it to those analyses, and the collection
to the dates they use, matched by name -- a deployed date is a copy, with
no link back to its collection row. `unassigned` as the project exports
from the analyses filed under no project, which need `analysis`.
List every date in this project's collection, oldest entry first.

post.description:
Add dates to this project's collection. Takes a list so the UI's
bulk-paste path is one request rather than N.

patch.description:
Apply one value across a selection of this project's dates. None of the
three is a plain assignment.

**curve_id** carries the sample type with it, since a date calibrated
against a marine curve is marine; the single-date form keeps the two in
step in the other direction.

**delta_r** is applied only to the marine dates in the selection, and the
response says how many were skipped. On a terrestrial date the offset is
not merely unnecessary but wrong -- it would be applied at calibration and
move the result. Skipping rather than refusing lets a mixed selection
work, which matters because "everything from this site" is how dates
sharing an offset are naturally selected.

**delta_r_source** rides with delta_r and is cleared by its absence. A ΔR
the lookup derived arrives with the record that reproduces it; a ΔR
somebody typed arrives without one, and that clears whatever was there.
Provenance surviving a hand edit would describe a number it did not
produce -- see §5.5 of the spatial plan.

**latitude/longitude** go to the whole selection, marine or not, because
where a date came from is a fact about the place rather than about the
material. This is the path the map's "place on map" uses: dates from one
site share a position, so a pin is one request.

`delta_r: null` clears the offset and its uncertainty, and a null
coordinate pair unplaces the selection; omitting the key leaves them
alone. The endpoint reads `model_fields_set` rather than checking for
None, so the two stay distinguishable.

Analyses already deployed from these dates are untouched.

delete.description:
Remove several dates from the collection at once.

All-or-nothing on the ids: an id not in this project fails the whole
request, because a caller cannot recover from a partial delete without
diffing the collection afterwards.

The ids travel in the body rather than the query string, which has a
length limit 500 uuids (about 18KB) would exceed. An intermediary that
strips the body produces a 422, not a silent no-op.

Analyses already deployed from these dates are unaffected.

get.description:
The collection as a CSV the date importer reads straight back in, every
stored field included (project_export.samples_csv). `sample` (repeatable)
narrows it to those dates. Positions leave at the project's coordinate
precision, as every export's do.

patch.description:
Edit a date in the collection. Analyses already deployed from it hold
their own copies and are untouched (see ProjectSample).

delete.description:
Remove a date from the collection. Analyses already deployed from it
keep their own copies and are unaffected.

post.description:
Create a new analysis in this project from a selection of its dates.

Each date's values are copied into a fresh RadiocarbonSample, and dates
sharing a default_context_name are grouped into one SampleGroup so they
arrive already organised into contexts. Everything is then editable
without touching the collection.

Created with status 'pending' -- inputs but no results. Run it with
POST /analysis/{id}/rerun, typically after adjusting its stratigraphy.

Deploying more than one date as `calibration` produces a
`group_calibration`; `data.analysis_type` reports the type created.

Parse an uploaded file of dates and return what it held, without saving
any of it.

Accepts a delimited table (.csv/.tsv/.txt) or an OxCal model (.oxcal).
The format is chosen by extension, falling back on the content itself --
see services/date_import.parse_upload.

The response carries three channels to show differently: `errors`
(nothing was imported), `warnings` (imported, but something could not be
honoured) and `notes` (imported, and here is what was assumed). See
services/date_import.ImportResult.

`async def` for the upload read only; parsing is blocking work and goes to
the threadpool.

get.description:
The CSV template, as a download.

Includes worked example rows rather than a bare header, since the column
names cannot say that delta_r requires its uncertainty, or that a residual
date is outlier_model 'charcoal' at prior 1.0.

The columns the CSV importer reads, for the upload dialog's format help.
Served rather than duplicated in the frontend so the help and the parser
cannot disagree.

post.description:
What a project package holds and what importing it would do, storing
nothing. Answers 200 for a package with problems, as /import/dates does:
the request worked, and its answer is `data.errors`.

Import a project package as a new project. Takes the file again rather
than the preview, for the reason POST /curves gives: the client is not a
route by which data reaches the database. Refused whole, with the
preview's errors, if anything in it is wrong.

Every analysis arrives 'pending'. POST /projects/{id}/rerun runs them.

Save a model's structure and settings as a template. Whatever names a
date or records a result is dropped, and the tree gets ids of its own.

patch.description:
Rename a template or change its description. Its structure does not
change: save the model again as a new template for that.

delete.description: Delete a template. Analyses built from it keep their own copy.

get.description:
Templates as one JSON file, which POST /import/model-templates reads
back in here or on another installation. `template` (repeatable) chooses
which; without it, all of them.

post.description:
What a templates file holds and what importing it would do. Answers
200 for a file with problems; its answer is `data.errors`.
Add a templates file's templates to this account, all or none.

get.description:
One job's state, progress and detail.

`state` is 'queued', 'running', 'completed', 'failed' or 'cancelled'.
Stop polling on the last three.

`progress` is a fraction, and for a sampled model an UPPER BOUND: the
sampler stops as soon as it converges, so most runs succeed well short of
1.0. `detail.convergence` says how well, and is the figure to show beside
a bar about to jump from 0.3 to done.

delete.description:
Ask a job to stop.

Cooperative and so not instant: a queued job is dropped before it starts,
a running one stops at its next checkpoint. The response says the request
was accepted, not that the job stopped -- poll for `state` to become
'cancelled'. A cancelled run writes nothing, so the analysis keeps the
results it had: a stop, not an undo.

get.description:
Recent jobs, newest first, optionally about one analysis or project.

`target_id` is what a bookmarked page uses: it has an analysis id and no
job id, and still needs to know whether something is running.

Every snapshot this account may use: the bundled ones, plus its own.

Someone else's ingested snapshot is not listed and not resolvable, exactly
as their imported curves are not. The bundled snapshot belongs to the
install and is listed for everyone.

post.description:
Fetch the marine reservoir database and store what comes back.

All-or-nothing: a fetch that does not parse cleanly writes nothing, and
the report lists every problem rather than the first. The report is the
response whether or not it succeeded, because the counts in it -- rows
with no uncertainty, cp1252 fallbacks, feeding spellings nobody has seen
-- are what a person needs to judge the source, not just the fetch.

503 when calib.org cannot be reached, which is a different thing from a
response that will not parse: one is a network to try again on, the other
is a source that has changed shape and needs a person to look at it.

get.description:
One snapshot's metadata, and whether it still verifies.

The verification is done here rather than reported from the row because a
row can only say what the hash was when it was written. Loading is what
checks it, and someone looking at this page is usually asking exactly
that question.

delete.description:
Remove an ingested snapshot, if nothing is citing it.

A bundled snapshot cannot be deleted at all -- it is a file that ships
with the app, and a route that appeared to delete one would be lying.

get.description:
What calib.org holds now, beside what this installation holds.

**Explicit, and only ever informational.** Nothing calls this on a timer or
on startup, and it never re-ingests: a ΔR that changed because a remote
database changed, underneath an analysis somebody has already published, is
exactly the failure the snapshot rules exist to prevent. The answer is an
invitation, and the button beside it is the decision.

It costs about 2 KB against the megabyte a full fetch costs, which is what
makes asking cheap enough to offer at all.

A 503 when the host cannot be reached is not an error state for the app:
the mirror already stored is unaffected, and this breaks refresh rather
than analysis.

post.description:
Derive a ΔR for a position from a snapshot, without telling anybody where
it is.

That is the whole point of the local mirror: this endpoint answers "what
reservoir measurements are near HERE" out of a table this installation
already has, where asking calib.org the same question would send a site's
coordinates to a third party on every lookup.

Returns the value AND what is needed to judge it -- the sigma, the N, the
distance to the nearest point, the point list with habits, and the
counterfactual with the biased habit classes dropped. The panel that shows
this is obliged to show them; see §11.3, which is the risk that a derived
number gets trusted more than it deserves.

Writes nothing. Applying a value is a separate, explicit act through the
bulk update, which is what records the provenance.

An order for the model's sites, read off a minimum spanning tree.

A proposal, never an application. The response carries the order, the tree
it was derived from, and a refusal in the user's own words when the model
has nothing to order -- fewer than two placed sites, or a phase holding
dates from two different places, which is a modelling error this refuses
to average over rather than silently working around.

get.description: The analysis's kept runs, newest (the current result) first.

One kept run in GET /analysis/{id}'s shape, so the comparison page reads
it as it reads an analysis. Its id is `analysis_id@run_id` and it carries
`run` (when, on what code, under what seed), so two runs of one analysis
can sit side by side; the page labels it in the reader's own time zone.

For every analysis in the project with two kept runs, what moved between
the latest and the one before it (diff_runs). Read after a project
re-run, it lists the analyses the re-run changed.

post.description:
Queue an influence run over the variants `kinds` asks for. Answers 202
with a job_id; the report is at GET .../influence once it completes.

get.description:
The last influence report, or null. `stale` is true when the analysis's
dates, model or settings have changed since it was made.

post.description:
Make one variant of the last report a saved analysis in the same project,
and queue its run: answers 202 with the new analysis's id and a job_id.

AnalysisBulkDelete.title: AnalysisBulkDelete
AnalysisBulkDelete.description: DELETE body for removing several analyses at once (api/analysis.py).

age_bp.title: Age Bp
age_bp.description: Radiocarbon age in years BP. Must be non-negative and within the range calibration curves cover (IntCal20/Marine20/SHCal20 span 0-55,000 cal BP).

error_1sigma.title: Error 1Sigma
error_1sigma.description: 1-sigma measurement uncertainty in years. Must be positive -- zero or negative error is not a valid measurement uncertainty.

BayesianMeasurementInput.title: BayesianMeasurementInput
BayesianMeasurementInput.description:
A measurement within a Bayesian analysis request. Needs a
client-supplied id so relationships can reference it.

age_bp.title: Age Bp
age_bp.description: Radiocarbon age in years BP. Must be non-negative and within the range calibration curves cover (IntCal20/Marine20/SHCal20 span 0-55,000 cal BP).

error_1sigma.title: Error 1Sigma
error_1sigma.description: 1-sigma measurement uncertainty in years. Must be positive -- zero or negative error is not a valid measurement uncertainty.

CurveMetadataUpdate.title: CurveMetadataUpdate
CurveMetadataUpdate.description:
Every field optional: a PATCH that names only `description` must not
blank the citation beside it.

DeployRequest.title: DeployRequest
DeployRequest.description:
POST body for deploying a project's dates into a new analysis (see
api/project_samples.py). The dates are COPIED, so the analysis is
independent of the collection from then on.

DispersalOrigin.title: DispersalOrigin
DispersalOrigin.description:
Where a wave of advance is hypothesised to have started.

Both halves required, unlike a sample's coordinates: a date with half a
position is a half-entered date, but an origin with half a position is not
an origin at all -- there is nothing to measure a distance from.

GroupCalibrationRequest.title: GroupCalibrationRequest
GroupCalibrationRequest.description:
Request body for POST /analysis/calibrate-group: unmodelled calibration
of several independent measurements, saved as one analysis so they share
the Results page's plot and table -- one timeline, no stratigraphic
relationship asserted. See BayesianRequest for that.

Reuses BayesianMeasurementInput so the UI can send the measurement objects
it already builds for a Bayesian draft unchanged. Its
group_id/element_id/outlier_* fields are accepted but not applied: a group
calibration has no phases and no outlier model to be an outlier from.

LookupRequest.title: LookupRequest
LookupRequest.description:
Where to look, and how widely.

The position is required and the rest have defaults, because the question
this answers is "what is the ΔR here" and everything else is a refinement
of it.

age_bp.title: Age Bp
age_bp.description: Radiocarbon age in years BP. Must be non-negative and within the range calibration curves cover (IntCal20/Marine20/SHCal20 span 0-55,000 cal BP).

error_1sigma.title: Error 1Sigma
error_1sigma.description: 1-sigma measurement uncertainty in years. Must be positive -- zero or negative error is not a valid measurement uncertainty.

MeasurementInput.title: MeasurementInput
MeasurementInput.description:
A single radiocarbon measurement.

The numeric bounds are generous sanity checks, not claims about
scientific validity: they catch data-entry mistakes (an extra digit, a
calendar year pasted into the BP field, a sign error) rather than
gatekeeping legitimate edge-case measurements.

percent_a.title: Percent A
percent_a.description: Percentage of the carbon from the first curve

MixedCurveRequest.title: MixedCurveRequest
MixedCurveRequest.description:
A curve defined as a proportional mixture of two others -- OxCal's
Mix_Curves.

The proportion is stated as a percentage of the FIRST curve, as OxCal
states it, so a recipe copied from an .oxcal file means the same thing
here. Its uncertainty is not optional in practice: a dietary fraction is
estimated, and an estimate offered without its error produces a mixed
curve that is more confident than the diet it came from.

ProjectSampleBulkDelete.title: ProjectSampleBulkDelete
ProjectSampleBulkDelete.description:
DELETE body for removing several dates from a project's collection.
Analyses deployed from them keep their own copies (models.ProjectSample).

ProjectSampleBulkInput.title: ProjectSampleBulkInput
ProjectSampleBulkInput.description:
POST body for adding dates to a project's collection -- a list, so the
UI's "paste several dates at once" path is a single request.

ProjectSampleBulkUpdate.title: ProjectSampleBulkUpdate
ProjectSampleBulkUpdate.description:
PATCH body for applying one value across a selection of a project's
dates -- the calibration curve, a Delta-R shared by everything from one
site or water body, or the coordinate those dates share, all of which are
per-provenance rather than per-date.

Whether a field was SENT matters, not whether it is null: `delta_r: null`
clears the offset, omitting the key leaves it alone. Pydantic records that
in `model_fields_set`, so no sentinel is needed -- see
api/project_samples.bulk_update_project_samples.

age_bp.title: Age Bp
age_bp.description: Radiocarbon age in years BP. Must be non-negative and within the range calibration curves cover (IntCal20/Marine20/SHCal20 span 0-55,000 cal BP).

error_1sigma.title: Error 1Sigma
error_1sigma.description: 1-sigma measurement uncertainty in years. Must be positive -- zero or negative error is not a valid measurement uncertainty.

ProjectSampleInput.title: ProjectSampleInput
ProjectSampleInput.description:
A date being added to a PROJECT's collection (models.ProjectSample):
every MeasurementInput check, plus the deploy-time context default.

ProjectSampleUpdate.title: ProjectSampleUpdate
ProjectSampleUpdate.description:
PATCH body for a date in a project's collection -- every field optional.
Constraints mirror ProjectSampleInput; the TPQ/TAQ ordering check cannot
be repeated here (a partial update may carry only one of the pair) and is
applied against the merged result in the endpoint.

ProposeSequenceRequest.title: ProposeSequenceRequest
ProposeSequenceRequest.description:
A draft model and its dates, as the tree editor holds them.

The tree and measurements come from the request rather than from the
database because this is offered on a DRAFT: there may be no saved
analysis yet, and the whole point is to propose an order before anything
has been run.

RelationshipInput.title: RelationshipInput
RelationshipInput.description:
A stratigraphic constraint between two nodes in a Bayesian analysis. Each
side is a measurement or a group, per from_type/to_type. The `relationship`
Literal is what rejects a typo like "beneath", which the constraint
builder would otherwise drop silently.

SameEventRequest.title: SameEventRequest
SameEventRequest.description:
Request body for POST /analysis/same-event: whether these measurements
could all date one event (services/statistics.same_event). Nothing is
saved -- the model editor asks it of a Phase's dates before they are run,
which is where the answer decides something.

SampleGroupInput.title: SampleGroupInput
SampleGroupInput.description:
A named stratigraphic phase/group within a Bayesian analysis request, so
one relationship or limiter applies to every member at once. Needs a
client-supplied id so relationships and measurements can reference it
before anything is persisted.

SimulateRequest.title: SimulateRequest
SimulateRequest.description:
A date asked for by calendar year rather than by measurement: what would a
sample from this year look like, measured this well?

HTTPBearer.description: A sign-in token from POST /api/auth/login, or a personal access token (rct_...) made on the Account page.
